title: How Historic Districts Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain historic districts in the United States. They start with Charleston, South Carolina, which created the first historic district with its Board of Architectural Review, followed by New Orleans' French Quarter. They trace the rise of preservation to highway construction and urban renewal, the National Historic Preservation Act of 1956, and the creation of the National Register of Historic Places in 1966. They cover the five resource categories (buildings, structures, objects, sites, districts), eligibility criteria (generally 50 years old, significance, historic context, integrity), contributing versus non-contributing properties, and how to pursue a national listing through the State Historic Preservation Officer. They explain that national listing offers limited federal protections, while local designation via preservation ordinances and commissions has real legal teeth, including design review and material requirements. They discuss pros and cons, including property values, tourism, gentrification and housing-cost criticism, Atlanta's Fox Theatre, and Old Town Alexandria. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about government shutdown effects and the sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to historic districts
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the clock tower and Back to the Future, distinguish a landmark building from a historic district, and introduce the idea that historic districts are charming, sometimes controversial, and numerous in the US.

segments.title: Charleston, New Orleans, and origins of historic districts
segments.summary: Charleston, South Carolina formed the first US historic district and its Board of Architectural Review. Within five years New Orleans protected the French Quarter. The concept grew out of highway construction and urban renewal in the 1950s, leading to the National Historic Preservation Act of 1956 and the National Register of Historic Places in 1966.

segments.title: National Register categories and eligibility criteria
segments.summary: The National Register lists buildings, structures, objects, sites, and districts, with an emphasis on place in the US. Resources generally must be 50 years old, significant, tied to historic context, and have integrity. Hosts give examples such as a grain elevator, Florida Southern College, and an archaeological site.

segments.title: Contributing and non-contributing properties
segments.summary: A historic district can include non-contributing properties, such as a modern house, without disqualifying the district. Integrity is judged by whether physical features still reflect the historic significance, so altered homes may be excluded.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before discussing the application process.

segments.title: Applying for National Register listing
segments.summary: Using an Atlanta neighborhood example, hosts explain that a homeowner should contact the State Historic Preservation Officer, who helps assess eligibility and complete forms. A state review board of architects, historians and archaeologists makes the decision. National listing gives limited federal protections, such as review when federal funding or projects are involved, but does not stop owners from neglecting property.

segments.title: Local historic districts, ordinances, and design review
segments.summary: Local designation has real teeth. A city needs a preservation ordinance and a preservation commission, public hearings are held, and majority support from owners and businesses is usually needed. Once designated, exterior repairs must follow historically accurate materials and approval from a local design review board, with penalties such as liens. A Maryland porch-column example is cited.

segments.title: Pros and cons of historic districts
segments.summary: Pros include stable or rising property values, tourism, and business draw. Cons include restrictions on owners, libertarian objections, and claims that preservation raises housing costs and drives gentrification. Kristen Capps' City Lab argument about zoning and housing inequality is discussed. Michigan lawmakers and varying local rules, such as Georgia and Old Town Alexandria, are noted.

segments.title: Atlanta urban renewal and the Fox Theatre
segments.summary: Hosts recall the Fox Theatre in Atlanta being nearly replaced by a bank parking lot in the 1970s and saved by a fundraising campaign. They discuss how 1950s and 1960s urban renewal tore down old buildings in downtown Atlanta, and how the city has more recently moved toward rehabilitation. Gentrification concerns are raised again.

segments.title: Closing discussion and resolution
segments.summary: Hosts note the topic's open-ended nature and invite listeners to try getting their own place listed and report back.

segments.title: Listener mail: government shutdown follow-up
segments.summary: A listener who works in federal government says the effects of past shutdowns lasted months, creating backlogs in agency work.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the website and email for contacting the show and note the iHeartRadio app and podcast sources.
